title: Google’s BERT: how fill-in-the-blank training teaches language understanding
summary: BERT trains a Transformer encoder on cloze tasks over 3.3 billion words, then adds one output layer to handle classification, question answering and tagging — breaking 11 records at once. We unpack its two pre-training tasks, input format and fine-tuning recipe, using worked examples and ablation results to show why it works and what problems remain.
ai_summary: BERT (Google AI Language, 2018) pre-trains a bidirectional Transformer encoder: it randomly masks 15% of word pieces for the model to predict (80% replaced with [MASK], 10% with random words, 10% unchanged) and has it decide whether two sentences are consecutive. Pre-training uses BooksCorpus plus English Wikipedia, 3.3 billion words total; BASE (110M parameters) and LARGE (340M parameters) each train for 4 days. Fine-tuning adds only an output layer and sets new records on 11 tasks: GLUE 80.5 (up 7.7), SQuAD v1.1 test F1 93.2, v2.0 83.1. Ablations show the gain comes mainly from bidirectionality; limitations include [MASK] appearing only in pre-training, predicting only 15% of tokens per batch, a 512-token input limit, and not suited to generation.
brief: Problem: earlier pre-trained models (GPT, ELMo) were unidirectional, so each word’s representation lacks context from the other side — a serious disadvantage for tasks like question answering.
Method: mask 15% of words and have the model predict them from both directions, plus a next-sentence prediction task; inputs are packed into a single sequence with [CLS] and [SEP].
Result: with only one added layer at fine-tuning, it set records on 11 tasks, raised GLUE by 7.7 points and SQuAD v2.0 by 5.1 points.
Lesson: at the same size, bidirectional beats unidirectional; bigger models help even on tasks with only a few thousand examples.

paper.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
paper.authors: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova

cover.headline: Inside the BERT paper
cover.highlight: Cloze tasks teach machines to understand language

sections.h: The bottom line: what the paper actually did

blocks.p: In October 2018, four researchers at Google AI Language introduced **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers). The recipe has two steps: first, a Transformer encoder repeatedly does fill-in-the-blank exercises over 3.3 billion words of books and Wikipedia text to learn language itself; then a small output layer is attached and tuned with a modest amount of labeled data for each specific task.

That simple recipe set records on 11 natural language processing tasks: the GLUE score climbed to 80.5, a jump of 7.7 points; SQuAD v1.1 test F1 reached 93.2 and v2.0 reached 83.1, the latter 5.1 points above the previous best system. More importantly, where each task used to need its own purpose-built architecture, BERT showed for the first time that **one pre-trained model plus one output layer can handle them all**.

If the Transformer from our previous close reading is the engine of large models, BERT is the paper that first proved the recipe “pre-train on huge unlabeled text, then fine-tune for a task” can work across the board. Today nearly all large models follow this pre-training → fine-tuning pipeline, even though the mainstream later shifted to GPT’s decoder-only line.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: BERT = a Transformer encoder (each word sees both left and right) + two pre-training tasks (predict 15% of masked words, decide whether two sentences are consecutive) + one unified recipe (the same model, with a different input format and one output layer, handles classification, QA and tagging).

callout.title: Four concepts to know before reading
callout.text: Don’t worry if they’re new; these four are enough:
list: **Transformer encoder**: the half of the architecture where self-attention lets each word see the whole sentence. See our previous close reading of “Attention Is All You Need.”
**Language model**: a model that predicts the next word from the preceding words. GPT is trained this way.

**Pre-training and fine-tuning**: first learn general language knowledge from huge amounts of unlabeled text (like reading widely), then practice on a small amount of labeled data for a specific task (like cramming with past exams).
**Labeled data**: examples with human-provided answers, such as “is this review positive or negative?” It is expensive and scarce; unlabeled text is almost limitless.

sections.h: Before BERT: two approaches, one shared weakness

blocks.p: By 2018 there were two main ways to use pre-trained models for downstream tasks, and the paper opens by laying them out:

list: **Feature-based**, exemplified by ELMo: pre-train a language model, then feed its word vectors into each task’s purpose-built model as extra features. The pre-trained model itself stays frozen.

**Fine-tuning**, exemplified by OpenAI’s GPT: pre-train a Transformer language model, add only a few new parameters for the downstream task, then retrain the whole model together with those new parameters.

blocks.p: The paper argues these two routes share the same weakness: **they both pre-train with unidirectional language models**. GPT reads left to right, so each word can see only the words to its left in self-attention. ELMo trains a left-to-right and a right-to-left model, but they are trained independently and simply concatenated; inside the model, left and right context are never truly fused.

callout.title: Why unidirectional hurts: an example
callout.text: Consider “my newly bought apple is delicious” and “my newly bought apple is really useful.” By the time the model reaches the word “apple,” the clue that decides whether it means the fruit or an Apple product comes later (delicious vs. useful). A left-to-right model cannot see those later words at that position and has to wait; yet many language-understanding tasks, such as finding where an answer lies in question answering, require every position to know both sides at once.

fig.title: Three pre-trained models compared: only BERT attends to both left and right in every layer
fig.subtitle: Based on Section 2 and Appendix A.4 of the paper. The amber row is BERT.
rows: Two LSTMs, one in each direction
Independently trained, concatenated at the end
Feature-based: freeze the model, extract features
Every layer attends to both sides

quiz.q: In “my newly bought apple is really useful,” what information can a left-to-right language model use when it processes the word “apple”?
quiz.why: At each position, a left-to-right model can see only itself and the words to its left. “Really useful” is to the right, so it isn’t visible when the model processes “apple,” and the model can’t tell at that point that apple means the device. This is why the paper says unidirectional models are at a disadvantage on tasks that need context from both sides.

sections.h: Why not just go bidirectional? The model would “see itself.”

blocks.p: If bidirectional is better, why didn’t anyone simply train a bidirectional language model? The paper gives a key explanation: standard language models can only be trained unidirectionally because with bidirectional attention **each word indirectly “sees itself”**, and the model could trivially guess the target word.

How exactly? Suppose the model has to predict the 5th word. In layer 1, positions 4 and 6 both attended to position 5 through self-attention. In layer 2, when position 5 attends to positions 4 and 6, it essentially gets its own answer back secondhand. With more layers, the answer leaks back from all directions, and the model learns to copy rather than understand language.

callout.title: It’s like having the answer printed next to the exam question.
callout.text: A left-to-right language model is safe because when predicting the 5th word, no position can see the 5th word or anything after it. Remove that restriction without any fix, and the answer is mixed into the question.

blocks.p: BERT’s solution is simple: **if the target word would leak, mask it first**. That is the first pre-training task.

sections.h: Task one: mask a word and predict it — the cloze task

blocks.p: The paper calls this **Masked LM** (MLM) and notes it’s usually called a cloze task in the literature (proposed back in 1953 to measure reading difficulty). The procedure: randomly choose 15% of the word pieces in a sentence, mask them, and ask the model to predict each original word from all the remaining context, left and right. The final-layer output at each masked position goes through a softmax over the whole vocabulary to score the correct word.

callout.title: What are word pieces?
callout.text: BERT doesn’t treat English words as whole units. It uses WordPiece to split words into smaller pieces with a vocabulary of 30,000. Common words stay intact; rare ones get split — in the paper’s figure, “playing” becomes “play” and “##ing” (where ## means the piece continues after the previous one). Masking is done on word pieces, not whole words.

blocks.p: But this creates a mismatch: [MASK] never appears during fine-tuning, so pre-training and fine-tuning don’t line up. The paper’s fix is not to replace all 15% of chosen positions with [MASK], but to handle them in three ways: 80%, 10%, 10%. The paper’s example is “my dog is hairy,” with “hairy” chosen:

fig.title: For each chosen word: 80% masked, 10% random, 10% unchanged
fig.subtitle: Example from Appendix A.1; no matter the treatment, the model must predict “hairy” at that position. The blue column is what the model actually sees.
rows: The main case: force the model to use context
Stop it from trusting the visible word
Keep representations close to real observed words

blocks.p: The clever part: the model never knows which positions will be tested or which words were replaced with random ones, so it has to keep a strong context-aware representation at every position instead of only trying when it sees [MASK]. Random replacements affect only 1.5% of all word pieces (10% × 15%), which the paper argues doesn’t hurt language understanding.

fig.title: Masking alternatives: fine-tuning is forgiving, but [MASK]-only clearly hurts feature-based use
fig.subtitle: From Table 8, dev-set results. The first row is BERT’s scheme; the amber row is “[MASK]-only.”
fig.note: MNLI is sentence-pair inference (accuracy); NER is named entity recognition (F1). In feature-based mode the model’s parameters stay frozen and only features are extracted, so any pre-training/fine-tuning mismatch can’t be corrected by fine-tuning; that’s why “[MASK]-only” hurts more there.

blocks.p: There’s another cost: a normal language model practices prediction at every position, while MLM predicts only 15% of words per batch, so it learns a bit more slowly. The appendix compares this directly: MLM converges slightly more slowly than a left-to-right model, but its accuracy surpasses the left-to-right model almost from the start.

quiz.q: In a 512-word-piece training sequence, about how many positions are selected for prediction under BERT’s rules, and about how many of them become random words?
options: About 77 predicted positions, about 8 of them random
quiz.why: 512 × 15% ≈ 77 positions are selected for prediction. Of those, 10% are replaced with random words: 77 × 10% ≈ 8, about 1.5% of all word pieces. Another 61 or so (80%) become [MASK], and about 8 stay unchanged.

quiz.q: Why not replace all selected 15% with [MASK]?
options: [MASK] never appears during fine-tuning, so mask-only would create a pre-training/fine-tuning mismatch; mixed treatment also forces the model to build good representations for every word
[MASK] would let the model see itself
The paper limits each sentence to one [MASK]
quiz.why: The paper says it’s explicitly to reduce the pre-training/fine-tuning mismatch. The appendix goes further: because the model doesn’t know which words will be tested or replaced, it must keep good contextual representations everywhere. Table 8 also shows “[MASK]-only” hurts most in feature-based use.

blocks.p: Many important tasks — question answering (how question and passage relate), natural language inference (whether the second sentence follows from the first) — need understanding of **relationships between two sentences**, while masked word prediction only exercises within-sentence structure. So the paper adds a second pre-training task: **Next Sentence Prediction** (NSP).

It’s just as simple and can be created for free from any text: each training sample pairs sentence A with sentence B. In 50% of cases, B is the actual next sentence after A (labeled IsNext); in the other 50%, B is a random sentence from the corpus (labeled NotNext). Two examples from the appendix:

fig.title: Next-sentence prediction: one is the true continuation, one is random
fig.subtitle: From Appendix A.1 (masking is also applied in both sentences)

blocks.p: The paper reports the final model reaches 97%–98% accuracy on NSP. Ablations (discussed later) show that removing NSP hurts QA and sentence-inference tasks significantly.

quiz.q: In NSP training data, true continuations and random sentences are evenly split. If a model learns nothing and always answers IsNext, what accuracy does it get? What does that suggest about the 97%–98% figure?
options: 50%; and because random sentences often have completely different topics, the task may be easier than it looks
100%, because most sentences are true continuations
quiz.why: Always guessing IsNext gets exactly half right. More importantly: NotNext sentences are randomly drawn and often discuss completely different topics (store vs. penguin), so a model can get most of them right simply by detecting topic coherence, without genuinely understanding sentence logic. This is exactly the avenue later research used to question NSP.

callout.title: What happened to NSP later
callout.text: The paper’s ablations support NSP. But later work (for example RoBERTa in 2019) found that with larger-scale training, dropping NSP doesn’t hurt — one likely reason being exactly what the question above suggests: random sentences are too easy to tell apart. When reading papers, remember that an ablation conclusion holds only under that paper’s own setup.

sections.h: How inputs are assembled: one sequence holds one or two sentences

blocks.p: To let one model handle many tasks, BERT packs every input into a single sequence: a special **[CLS]** token at the start, with **[SEP]** separators between sentences and at the end. Here a “sentence” isn’t necessarily a grammatical sentence; it can be any span of continuous text, up to 512 word pieces.

At each position, the input vector is the **sum** of three vectors: the token embedding for the word itself, a segment embedding indicating sentence A or B, and a position embedding for its position. Unlike the original Transformer, which uses sinusoidal functions for positions, BERT learns its position and segment embeddings.

fig.title: Input vector = token embedding + segment embedding + position embedding
fig.subtitle: Redrawn from Figure 2 (first 7 positions). E is a learnable vector; the subscript indicates what it corresponds to.
fig.note: The full example is [CLS] my dog is cute [SEP] he likes play ##ing [SEP], 11 positions total; all segment embeddings in the second half are E_{B}.

blocks.p: The final-layer output for [CLS] (denoted C in the paper) serves as a summary of the whole sequence and is used for classification and NSP. The output Tᵢ at every other position corresponds to that word and is used for token-level tasks such as QA and tagging.

callout.title: The [CLS] vector isn't a ready-made sentence representation
callout.text: Many people take a pre-trained BERT and use the [CLS] output directly as a sentence embedding to compute similarity. A footnote in the paper explicitly warns that, before fine-tuning, C is not a meaningful sentence representation, because during pre-training it was only used for NSP. To use it, you need to fine-tune it on a specific task first.

blocks.p: BERT's architecture is the original Transformer encoder; the paper says its implementation is "almost identical to the original," so it doesn't describe the model again in detail. It uses L for the number of layers, H for the hidden size, and A for the number of attention heads, with the feed-forward width set to 4H throughout. It mainly reports two sizes:

fig.title: BERT's two sizes, compared with other contemporary large models mentioned in the paper
fig.subtitle: From Sections 3 and 5.2 of the paper. The amber rows are BERT.
rows: Largest in the original Transformer (encoder part)
Largest Transformer mentioned in the paper's related work
fig.note: BERT-BASE's feed-forward width is 3072; LARGE's is 4096.

blocks.p: BERT-BASE was deliberately sized to match OpenAI GPT for a fair comparison. The paper stresses that the two are almost identical architecturally; the only critical difference is that BERT uses bidirectional self-attention, while GPT uses constrained self-attention where each token can attend only to its left. A footnote also explains the naming convention that later became standard: the bidirectional version is usually called a "Transformer encoder," and the left-only version a "Transformer decoder," because it can be used to generate text.

list: **Data**: BooksCorpus (800M words) plus English Wikipedia (2.5B words). For Wikipedia, only text passages are used; lists, tables, and headers are discarded. The paper stresses that a document-level corpus is essential, not a shuffled sentence-level corpus, because you need to draw long contiguous sequences from it, and next-sentence prediction requires real context.
**Scale**: 256 sequences × 512 word pieces per batch = 128,000 word pieces per batch, for 1,000,000 steps. That amounts to roughly 40 passes over the 3.3-billion-word corpus.

**Optimization**: Adam with learning rate 1e-4, a 10,000-step warm-up followed by linear decay; dropout 0.1 in all layers; GELU activation instead of ReLU (same as OpenAI GPT). The loss is the sum of the masked-word prediction and next-sentence prediction losses.
**Compute**: BASE uses 16 TPU chips and LARGE uses 64, with training taking 4 days in each case.

blocks.p: One detail directly echoes our previous close reading: the paper says long sequences are disproportionately expensive because attention computation grows quadratically with sequence length. So it used sequences of length 128 for the first 90% of training steps and switched to length 512 for the final 10%, mainly so the model would learn the position embeddings for those later positions. The n² problem from the Transformer paper is already shaping engineering choices here.

quiz.q: If attention cost scales quadratically, about how many times more attention computation does a length-512 sequence require compared with a length-128 sequence?
quiz.why: The length quadruples (512 / 128 = 4), and the number of pairwise attention comparisons grows to 4² = 16 times as many. This is why the paper trains with short sequences for most steps. Keep in mind this applies only to the attention part; feed-forward computation grows only linearly with sequence length.

sections.h: Fine-tuning: add one layer and handle every task

blocks.p: Once pre-training is done, adapting BERT to a specific task is straightforward: pack the task's input into BERT in the format described above, attach a layer to the appropriate output, and retrain **all parameters** together on that task's labeled data. Different tasks start from the same pre-trained parameters and each ends up with its own fine-tuned model.

fig.title: Four task types, one BERT: the only differences are how inputs are assembled and which output is used
fig.subtitle: Based on Section 3.2 and Appendix Figure 4.
rows: MNLI: whether the second sentence follows from the first
SST-2: whether a review is positive or negative
SQuAD: find the answer in a passage
Start vector S, end vector E
NER: label names of people and places

blocks.p: The classification formula is very short:

parts.desc: The final-layer output for [CLS], a length-H vector that represents the entire input.
The only new parameter is a matrix of shape K × H, where K is the number of classes (an inference task has three, for example: entailment, contradiction, neutral).
It turns K scores into K probabilities; during training, you maximize the log-probability of the correct class.

blocks.p: Question answering is a little more involved but just as elegant. Fine-tuning adds only two vectors: a start vector S and an end vector E. The dot product of each passage token's output Tᵢ with S gives the score that "the answer starts here":

formula.expr:
P_{start}(i) = e^{S·T_{i}} / Σ_{j} e^{S·T_{j}}
Candidate answer (i, j) score = S·T_{i} + E·T_{j}, with j ≥ i

parts.desc: The final-layer output of the i-th token in the passage.
The two vectors learned during fine-tuning; they rate how start-like or end-like a position is.
The end cannot come before the start; the span with the highest score is chosen as the answer.

formula.note: The training objective maximizes the sum of the log-probabilities of the correct start and correct end.

fig.title: Worked example: find the answer to "Where is the cat sitting?" in a passage
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the scores are invented, not from the paper. The passage tokens are "cat sits soft cushion on sleeping."
fig.note: The best-scoring span starts at "soft" and ends at "cushion": 3.1 + 2.9 = 6.0, so the answer is "soft cushion." An end position before "soft" would violate j ≥ i.

blocks.p: SQuAD 2.0 adds cases where the passage contains no answer. BERT's handling is just as simple: it treats "no answer" as a special answer where both the start and end fall on [CLS], with score S·C + E·C. It outputs a real answer only when the best real answer's score exceeds that no-answer score by a threshold τ, which is tuned on the dev set to maximize F1.

Compared with pre-training, fine-tuning is negligible. The paper says every result starts from the same pre-trained model and can be replicated in at most 1 hour on a single Cloud TPU, or a few hours on a GPU; for example, the SQuAD model reaches 91.0 F1 on the dev set in about 30 minutes. All GLUE tasks use batch size 32 and 3 epochs. BERT-LARGE can, however, be unstable when fine-tuned on small datasets, so the authors retry with several random initializations and pick the best dev-set run.

quiz.q: When fine-tuning BERT-LARGE on SQuAD v1.1, how many new parameters are added beyond BERT’s own parameters?
options: 2 × 1024 = 2,048 (start vector S and end vector E)
quiz.why: The paper says explicitly that QA fine-tuning introduces only a start vector S and an end vector E, each of length H. For LARGE, H = 1024, so that’s 2,048 new parameters in total; the other 340M parameters come from pre-training and are also updated during fine-tuning. That’s what “add one layer” really means.

sections.h: The scorecard: new records on all 11 tasks

callout.title: What are GLUE and SQuAD?
list: **GLUE**: a collection of nine language-understanding tasks, including sentence relationships, sentiment, grammatical acceptability, and whether two sentences mean the same thing. The paper excludes WNLI, which has issues, and reports the other eight.

**SQuAD**: Stanford's reading comprehension dataset: given a Wikipedia passage and a question, the model must select the answer span in the passage. v1.1 contains about 100,000 question–answer pairs; v2.0 adds questions where the passage has no answer.
**F1**: measures how much the predicted answer overlaps with the gold answer, scored out of 100; **EM** is the exact-match rate.

fig.title: GLUE eight-task average: BERT-BASE already beats GPT by 4.5 points
fig.subtitle: Units: points, GLUE test set, excluding WNLI. Amber bars are BERT; BERT-BASE has nearly the same architecture and size as GPT.
fig.note: From Table 1 of the paper. This average uses a slightly different method from the official GLUE score; on the official leaderboard, BERT-LARGE is 80.5 and GPT is 72.8.

fig.title: The less data a task has, the more BERT improves
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 (GLUE test set). Parentheses show training examples; blue columns are BERT-LARGE.
fig.note: For MNLI, only the matched set is shown. The improvement column is computed by subtracting the numbers in the paper's table.

blocks.p: On reading comprehension, the BERT-LARGE ensemble (fine-tuned first on TriviaQA, then on SQuAD) scored 93.2 F1 on the SQuAD v1.1 test set, 1.5 points above the best ensemble on the leaderboard at the time; a single model already beat the best ensemble. The paper also says that without TriviaQA it loses only 0.1–0.4 F1. On SQuAD v2.0, a single BERT-LARGE reached 83.1 F1, 5.1 points above the previous best system.

fig.title: Three reading and commonsense tasks: versus previous best and humans
fig.subtitle: Test sets, from Tables 2–4 of the paper; human scores are from each leaderboard or dataset paper. Blue columns are BERT.

callout.title: "Beating humans" depends on exactly what you compare
callout.text: On SQuAD v1.1, BERT's F1 beats the human score shown in the table, but that "human score" is a crowd-sourced baseline from the leaderboard, and every answer in v1.1 is guaranteed to be in the passage. On v2.0, which adds unanswerable questions, BERT's 83.1 is clearly below the human 89.5. A single number above a human baseline does not mean the model has surpassed humans at reading comprehension.

blocks.p: On SWAG — given a sentence, choose the most plausible continuation from four candidates — BERT-LARGE beats the dataset authors' baseline by 27.1 points and GPT by 8.3 points.

sections.h: Ablations: what actually accounts for the gains

blocks.p: Apart from bidirectionality, BERT and GPT differ in more ways: BERT uses more data (GPT used only BooksCorpus), larger batches, and learns [SEP], [CLS], and segment embeddings during pre-training. The appendix frankly lists these differences and uses ablations to answer where the improvements mainly come from.

fig.title: Remove next-sentence prediction, then go unidirectional: QA drops hardest
fig.subtitle: From Table 5, dev set; all use the BERT-BASE architecture and the same data. Blue columns are SQuAD.

blocks.p: Three things stand out. First, removing NSP clearly hurts QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD. Second, switching from bidirectional to left-to-right (row 3 — with the same data and fine-tuning, roughly GPT's recipe) makes every task worse; MRPC and SQuAD drop the most, with SQuAD falling from 87.9 to 77.8. The paper's explanation is intuitive: a left-to-right model has no right-side context in each word's representation, and locating the answer is exactly the kind of task that needs it. Third, stacking a bidirectional LSTM on top of the unidirectional model brings SQuAD back up to 84.9, but it's still far behind true bidirectional pre-training and actually worse on GLUE tasks.

The paper also addresses whether you could train two unidirectional models and combine them, as ELMo does. It costs twice as much as one bidirectional model; it's unnatural for QA because a right-to-left model cannot understand the answer conditioned on the question; and it's strictly less powerful, since a deep bidirectional model can use both left and right context at every layer.

fig.title: Bigger is better—even on tasks with only 3,600 training examples
fig.subtitle: Unit: MNLI dev-set accuracy (average of 5 fine-tuning runs). From Table 6; amber bars are BERT-BASE and BERT-LARGE.
fig.note: In the same table, MRPC — with only 3,600 training examples — also climbs from 79.8 to 87.8.

blocks.p: The paper argues this is the first convincing demonstration that **scaling models up yields large gains even on small tasks**, provided the model has been sufficiently pre-trained. Earlier feature-based work had mixed results on whether larger models help; the authors' guess is that when you fine-tune directly and add only a few parameters, the downstream task can fully benefit from the larger, more expressive pre-trained representation, even with little task data. The appendix adds that pre-training for 1 million steps instead of 500,000 improves MNLI by nearly 1 percentage point.

callout.title: Fine-tuning isn't the only way to use BERT
callout.text: Section 5.3 also tries the feature-based route: freeze BERT's parameters, treat intermediate-layer outputs as features, and feed them into a small model for named entity recognition. Concatenating the last four layers (96.1 dev F1) is only 0.3 points below fine-tuning the whole model (96.4). This route is cheaper when you need to run many experiments, or when a task doesn't fit neatly into a Transformer.

quiz.q: In Table 5, which change causes the largest drop in SQuAD performance, and what does that tell you?
options: Removing next-sentence prediction — meaning NSP is BERT's most important part
Switching from bidirectional to left-to-right — meaning token-level tasks especially depend on right-side context
Adding a bidirectional LSTM — meaning LSTM hurts
All three changes have equal impact
quiz.why: Removing NSP takes SQuAD from 88.5 to 87.9. On top of that, switching to left-to-right sends it from 87.9 to 77.8 — the biggest drop in the table. Question answering requires judging whether each position is an answer start or end, so each word needs to know what is to its right. That is exactly the value of bidirectionality.

sections.h: What BERT didn't solve, and what came next

list: **Pre-training/fine-tuning mismatch**: [MASK] appears only during pre-training; the 80/10/10 split is a mitigation, not a cure. Also, only 15% of words are predicted per batch, so training is less efficient.
**Dubious value of next-sentence prediction**: as noted earlier, later work at larger scale found that dropping NSP doesn't hurt.
**Length limit**: inputs are capped at 512 word pieces, still because of the quadratic cost of attention.

**Not built for generation**: BERT is an encoder, good at "reading" but with no natural token-by-token way to generate text. The paper itself notes in a footnote that the left-only "decoder" is the one suited to text generation.
**Unstable fine-tuning on small datasets**: BERT-LARGE needs several random restarts on small datasets to pick a good result.

blocks.p: After BERT, "pre-training + fine-tuning" quickly became the standard NLP recipe, and improved variants proliferated. But the main line leading to today's chat models took a different path: the GPT family stuck with the left-to-right language model and kept scaling both model and data. By GPT-3 (2020), many tasks no longer needed fine-tuning at all — a few examples in the prompt were enough. Those papers are on our reading list, and we'll cover them one by one.

callout.title: What to read next
callout.text: GPT-3's "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" covers doing tasks without fine-tuning; "Scaling Laws" covers just how regular the bigger-is-better trend is. Both are on the paper reading list.

sections.h: Test yourself: do you really understand it?

quiz.q: What is the most critical architectural difference between BERT and GPT?
options: BERT uses an LSTM, GPT uses a Transformer.
BERT’s self-attention attends to both left and right; GPT’s tokens can attend only to the left.
BERT has 10 times as many parameters as GPT.
quiz.why: The paper deliberately made BERT-BASE the same size as GPT and stressed that the two architectures are nearly identical; the difference is in attention masking: BERT is bidirectional, GPT is left-only. That difference is also what forced BERT to switch to masked word prediction.

callout.title: After reading, you should be able to answer these five questions in your own words.
list: Where do unidirectional language models fall short on understanding tasks? Give an example.
Why can’t you simply make a language model bidirectional? How does masked word prediction get around this?
Why are chosen words handled in three ways: 80%, 10%, and 10%?
How can the same BERT be used for three different kinds of tasks: classification, question answering, and token-level tagging?
